title: The tainted altruism effect: a successful pre-registered replication

source.title: The tainted altruism effect: a successful pre-registered replication
source.authors: Valerie Alcala, Kendra Johnson, Caroline Steele, Juanshu Wu, Donglai Zhang, and Harold Pashler

studies.title: Experiment 1: evaluating a business owner
studies.description: Replicates Newman and Cain’s Experiment 3. The shared Prolific cohort first evaluates a business owner.

studies.title: Experiment 2: choosing a fundraiser
studies.description: Replicates Newman and Cain’s Experiment 2. The same cohort next makes hypothetical hiring choices and rates the fundraiser.

nodes.title: When does doing good make someone look worse?

fields.label: Research question
fields.value: Does mixing a personal profit motive with a charitable act reduce approval compared with pursuing profit alone, and does this pattern extend to hypothetical choices?

fields.label: Why replicate?
fields.value: The authors preregistered a larger-sample replication of two of Newman and Cain’s experiments that illustrate the effect.

nodes.title: Predictions about the business owner

fields.label: Charity penalty
fields.value: The same publicity-driven business owner should be rated less favorably for donating money than for buying advertising.

fields.label: Role of the alternative action
fields.value: Making the opposite action explicit was expected to weaken or reverse the basic effect.

nodes.title: Predictions about the promoter

fields.label: Hiring intentions
fields.value: The study tests whether participants forgo more money for their own organization to avoid hiring a promoter who would earn a substantial profit, especially in a charitable context.

nodes.title: One Prolific cohort across both experiments

fields.label: Participants
fields.value: The authors report recruiting 501 U.S. residents (mean age 46.3; 51% female and 49% male) through Prolific, with strata for age, sex and ethnicity.

fields.label: Order across the paper
fields.value: The same cohort completed Experiment 2 after Experiment 1.

nodes.title: Donation or advertising, with or without a counterfactual

fields.label: Between-participant groups
fields.value: Participants were randomly assigned to one of four versions crossing how the money was spent with whether a sentence described the opposite spending option.

nodes.title: Charitable or corporate fundraiser

fields.label: Between-participant groups
fields.value: Participants were randomly assigned to imagine running either a charity or a corporation. Each participant made several choices in their assigned setting.

nodes.title: The Mulberry vignettes and ratings

fields.label: What participants read
fields.value: Frank Mulberry seeks good publicity and more customers by donating to a children’s hospital or buying advertising. In two versions the alternative action was stated explicitly.

fields.label: What participants rated
fields.value: Four items asked about ethics, approval, liking, and whether Mulberry acted as altruistically as he could. The replication added a fifth item asking about deceptiveness.

nodes.title: The Daniel P. fundraiser tasks

fields.label: What participants read
fields.value: Daniel P. runs a for-profit promotion company. Participants imagine choosing his company or another promoter for their charity or corporation.

fields.label: The first pair and the scored series
fields.value: The supplement supplies 12 choice pairs. The first offers a strictly better alternative to Daniel P.; it matches the paper’s description of a comprehension check before the 11 other choices.
fields.derivation: Matched the only dominated Daniel P. option at the start of the supplement to the paper’s description of the separate comprehension check.

nodes.title: Read one vignette and rate the owner

fields.label: Participant flow
fields.value: Read the assigned vignette, then rate the business owner using the paper’s 1–9 scale.

nodes.title: Choose between promoters and rate Daniel P.

fields.label: Participant flow
fields.value: Participants received the story and fundraising role, made the hiring choices in fixed order on one scrolling page, then rated Daniel P.

nodes.title: Action and counterfactual as inputs, ratings as outcomes

fields.label: Manipulated variables
fields.value: Charity versus advertising and counterfactual absent versus present.

fields.label: Outcomes
fields.value: Average of ethics, approval and liking items, alongside separate altruism and exploratory deceptiveness ratings.

nodes.title: Fundraiser type as input, hiring and ratings as outcomes

fields.label: Manipulated variable
fields.value: Charity versus corporation.

fields.label: Outcomes
fields.value: Hiring choices and two ratings composites. Morality averages ethics, morality and approval. Perceived benefit averages benefit and making the world a better place.

nodes.title: Liking contrasts and exploratory ratings

fields.label: Analyses reported
fields.value: The authors compared the charity and advertising groups with and without the counterfactual, tested their interaction in a 2 × 2 ANOVA, and described separate altruism and exploratory deceptiveness results.

nodes.title: Rating contrasts, exclusions and hiring curves

fields.label: Analyses reported
fields.value: The paper compares charity and corporate ratings and plots hiring shares by the benefit to the organization. It repeats rating contrasts without the two task-related exclusions.

fields.label: Main analysis exclusions
fields.value: The paper attributes 123 exclusions to choosing the dominated offer and 26 further exclusions to an alternative–Daniel–alternative pattern across ordered choices.

nodes.title: Liking reverses with an explicit alternative

fields.label: Without counterfactual
fields.value: Charity received lower liking than advertising (M = 5.28 versus 6.76; t(206) = 6.82, p < .001; reported Cohen’s d = 0.84).

fields.label: With counterfactual
fields.value: Charity received higher liking than advertising (M = 6.56 versus 5.58; t(226) = −4.29, p < .001). The interaction was F(1, 490) = 63.12, p < .001.

nodes.title: Altruism ratings show the same crossover descriptively

fields.label: Altruism ratings
fields.value: The four means were 3.98 for Charity, 4.96 for Advertising, 5.28 for Charity with Counterfactual, and 3.34 for Advertising with Counterfactual. The authors describe a crossover pattern.

nodes.title: Deceptiveness decreases without a crossover

fields.label: Exploratory ratings
fields.value: Without a counterfactual, Charity was rated more deceptive than Advertising (t(238) = 6.24, p < .001). Adding the counterfactual to Charity lowered the rating to 4.34 (t(232) = 2.22, reported p = .014). The authors report no reversal.

fields.label: Interpreting the duplicated mean
fields.value: The prose repeats 5.06 after the Advertising mean of 3.36. Figure 3 puts Advertising near 3.36 and Charity near 5.06.
fields.derivation: Compared the published text on both pages with the figure’s plotted means and legend.

nodes.title: Morality differs, perceived benefit does not

fields.label: After the reported exclusions
fields.value: Charity was rated lower for morality than Corporation (M = 5.16 versus 5.74; t(343) = 2.64, reported p = .004). Perceived benefit showed no significant difference (5.56 versus 5.47; p = .69).

fields.label: Without the reported exclusions
fields.value: The lower Charity morality rating persisted (M = 5.40 versus 5.92; p = .004). Benefit still did not differ significantly (M = 5.75 versus 5.72; p = .89).

nodes.title: The charity context shifts hypothetical hiring

fields.label: Observed choice pattern
fields.value: The authors report that participants in the Charity condition were more willing to pass up greater funds to avoid hiring Daniel P. Figure 4 shows lower selection of Daniel P. in Charity across the plotted extra-amount levels. The paper reports this pattern descriptively.

nodes.title: Mixed motives affected social judgments and intended choices

fields.label: Paper’s interpretation
fields.value: The authors conclude that the main results of the two earlier experiments were closely replicated. The counterfactual comparison qualified the liking effect, and the fundraiser result applied to morality and hypothetical hiring, with no reliable benefit-rating difference.

nodes.title: What the reconstruction can establish

fields.label: Possible explanation
fields.value: Deceptiveness is a possible explanation raised by the paper. The exploratory rating is evidence about perceptions, and the authors identify the mechanism as a question for future work.

evidence.quote: Newman & Cain [1] described a phenomenon they termed ‘tainted altruism’—when an ostensibly prosocial action also serves some private goal, the action is viewed as less virtuous than a purely selfish act.

Our project aimed to replicate two of Newman and Cain’s studies which seem to us to well embody these authors’ fundamental claims regarding the tainted altruism effect. We used a considerably larger sample than the original article and the study was pre-registered to pin down our research hypothesis, methods and analysis plans before the data collection commenced.
Our replication was pre-registered on AsPredicted.com where it can be accessed through this link: https://aspredicted.org/~7E94fcbelU.

In this experiment, participants were randomly assigned to one of four groups. In the first and second groups, the participants read a short passage in which a business owner either donated money to charity (Charity condition) or invested the money in advertising (Advertising condition) with the goal of increasing revenues for his business.
The basic tainted altruism effect consisted in people offering a lower evaluation of Mulberry in the Charity condition as compared with the Advertising condition.

Specifically, the authors surmised that the basic tainted altruism effect might be nullified or reversed if language were added to the vignettes that would lead participants to contrast Mulberry with a hypothetical oppositely motivated decision maker.

The passage that participants in the Charity condition read was: Frank Mulberry is the owner of a large chain of ‘Mulberry’s’ department stores located throughout the Midwest. Recently, Mulberry donated several million dollars to a local children’s hospital in Omaha, Nebraska, where his company is based. Mulberry donated the money because he knew that the good publicity would boost the reputation of his company and get more people to come to his stores.
to, Mulberry could have instead donated the money to charity. This would have also increased the reputation of his company, but all of the money would have gone to charity.

In the Charity with Counterfactual condition, subjects read (again, the added language is shown in italics): Frank Mulberry is the owner of a large chain of ‘Mulberry’s’ department stores located throughout the Midwest. Recently, Mulberry donated several million dollars to a local children’s hospital in Omaha, Nebraska, where his company is based. Mulberry donated the money because he knew that the good publicity would boost the reputation of his company and get more people to come to his stores. Keep in mind that if he wanted to, Mulberry could have instead invested the money in advertising. This would have also increased the reputation of his company, but none of the money would have gone to charity.

In all conditions, participants rated Mulberry’s behaviour on various dimensions using a 9-point scale (1 = absolutely not to 9 = absolutely). Participants were asked the following questions: ‘How ethical is Mulberry?’, ‘How much do you approve of Mulberry’s behaviour?’, ‘How much do you like Mulberry?’, and ‘Did Mulberry act as altruistically as he could have?’. One additional question (not included in the original study) was asked in our experiment on an exploratory basis: ‘How deceptive do you think Mulberry is?’ (our reasons for including this are described below).

Five hundred and one participants (mean age = 46.3 years, 51% female, 49% male) were recruited through Prolific.org, providing us with a representative sample of people residing in the US with regard to age, sex and ethnicity [7]. During the subject recruiting process, Prolific used three prescreeners: ‘Date of Birth’, ‘Sex’, and ‘Ethnicity (Simplified)’ to stratify age using five 9-year brackets (18–27, 28–37, 38–47, 48–57 and 58+), sex using male and female category and Ethnicity using five categories (White, Mixed, Asian, Black and Other). Six subjects failed an ‘attention check’ by neglecting to follow an explicit instruction about how to respond to an item included to assess attentiveness.
The same 501 participants completed the questions included in this experiment after completing the first experiment.

We defined the difference between the averaged liking ratings from the Charity and Advertising conditions (without counterfactual information) as the basic effect of tainted altruism. An unusually large effect size of Cohen’s d = 0.84 was observed for the effect (Charity versus Advertising without counterfactual information in either). The contrast of the two conditions was significant, t206 = 6.82, p < 0.001.

However, as shown in figure 1, when the counterfactual information was provided, the effects of condition (charity versus advertising) on liking was reversed, such that participants rated the target more positively when he gave to charity than when he invested the same money in advertising, t226 = −4.29, p < 0.001. A 2 × 2 analysis of variance revealed a significant interaction between domain (charity, advertising) and the presence/absence of counterfactual information, F1,490 = 63.12, p < 0.001. As figure 1 illustrates, the cross-over interaction found in our study closely resembled the corresponding interaction in the original study.

As to the question of how altruistically Mulberry acted, the average values were Charity = 3.98 (s.e. = 0.22), Advertising = 4.96 (s.e. = 0.18), Charity with Counterfactual = 5.28 (s.e. = 0.24) and Advertising with Counterfactual = 3.34 (s.e. = 0.19). The same pattern of cross-over interaction was evident as with the liking questions. This is shown in figure 2.

Our results confirmed the effect of the condition manipulation on perceptions of deceptiveness: Mulberry was rated significantly more deceptive in the Charity condition (M = 5.06) than in the Advertising

condition (3.36) (M = 5.06), t238 = 6.24, p < 0.001. Furthermore, when participants are reminded that Mulberry either could have acted charitably or did not have to act charitably by the counterfactual information, Mulberry was seen as less deceptive for donating to charity (M = 4.34), t232 = 2.22, p = 0.014. Interestingly, there was no reversal of the effect, however.

Deceptiveness ratings in the current replication study as a function of condition (Advertising versus Charity) and absence/ presence of the counterfactual information. Error bars represent standard error of the mean.

evidence.quote: The aim of this experiment was to determine whether the tainted-altruism effect would extend to participants’ behavioural intentions as reported in the original paper. Specifically, to quote the original investigator, the design examined whether people were ‘willing to forgo the opportunity to earn more money for a charity if the person raising the money also earned a substantial profit’ [1].

Participants were randomly assigned to one of two between-subjects conditions labelled Charity or Corporation. Participants were asked to imagine that they were the head of either a charity or a corporation, charged with the responsibility of choosing a promoter to raise funds for their organization.
Eleven binary hiring choices were then presented to participants (Newman and Cain stated that they used 10 choices but the supplementary materials showed 11).

The order in which these questions were asked was fixed across subjects (see electronic supplementary material for verbatim details). All these binary choices were presented on the same web page which participants scrolled down to view (submitting the web page when they were ready). We confirmed with the original authors that this matched the procedure of the original study (Newman, 21 April 2021, personal communication). After making their hypothetical hiring decisions, participants were asked to rate Daniel P. across several measures.

Following the original study, participants’ data were excluded if either of two conditions were held. The first was if they failed an initial comprehension check question (excluding 123 subjects). The second was if their set of choices violated an order constraint specified in the original study (excluding another 26), described further below. A total of 149 subjects’ data were excluded.

The comprehension check was a single binary hiring decision question presented before the eleven binary hiring questions that comprised this experiment. In this comprehension check, participants were asked to choose between Daniel P.’s firm who charged more and earned less than that of an alternative promoter which charged less and earned more. Participants who selected Daniel P.’s firm (an indefensible choice regardless of the relative importance of the two factors) were excluded from the data analysis. As in the original experiment, other participants were also excluded from data analysis if they made choices that broke a rather subtle ordering constraint. Specifically, a participant was excluded if they chose the alternative firm on question n, switched to choosing Daniel’s firm on some later question n + j (for some positive integer j), and then switched back to choosing the alternative firm on question n + k (for some positive integer k > j).

Responses to the first three rating questions were averaged together to produce a single measure of morality and the last two rating questions were averaged to produce a single measure of perceived benefit. The Cronbach’s alpha values were 0.927 for the morality questions and 0.844 for the benefit questions.

Participants in the charity condition rated Daniel P. as significantly less moral (M = 5.16, s.e. = 0.16) than did participants in the corporate condition (M = 5.74, s.e. = 0.15), t343 = 2.64, p = 0.004. Ratings of perceived benefit did not differ significantly across the two conditions, M = 5.56, s.e. = 0.16 for the Charity condition and M = 5.47, s.e. = 0.15 for the Corporate condition (t343 = 0.40, p = 0.69).

Without any data exclusion, for the morality measure, the means were 5.92 and 5.40 for Corporate and Charity conditions, respectively, a significant difference in the expected direction, t495 = 2.89, p = 0.004. This paralleled the results found with exclusion. For the benefit measure, the means were 5.72 and 5.75 for Corporate and Charity conditions, respectively. As with the results after data exclusion, this too yielded no significant difference between conditions, t495 = 0.14, p = 0.89.
Lines show the percentage of participants in each condition who selected Daniel’s firm as a function of the extra amount Daniel’s firm earned (and whether the condition was Corporate or Charity).

evidence.quote: participants in the Charity condition were willing to forgo the opportunity to make more money for their charity than they were willing to forgo in the Corporate condition (figure 4).
In Newman and Cain’s second experiment, 23% of their participants were excluded and in our replication, 30% of participants were excluded for the same reasons.
The analysis code for this study is public at https://figshare.com/s/f67f46b85cf9a756be7a.
To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first direct replication of any of the experiments in Newman & Cain’s [1] study on tainted altruism. Using a larger sample size and a US sample
intended to be fairly representative of the US population at least with respect to age, sex and ethnicity, we readily reproduced the main results in the original studies quite closely.

Now that the solidity of the tainted altruism effect seems well established, future research might explore the cause and mechanism of the effect in greater detail, addressing why and how a selfish motive undermines the judgement of prosocial behaviour.

evidence.quote: In the Advertising condition, the passage read: Frank Mulberry is the owner of a large chain of ‘Mulberry’s’ department stores located throughout the Midwest. Recently, Mulberry invested several million dollars in an extensive advertising campaign in Omaha, Nebraska, where his company is based. Mulberry invested the money because he knew that the good publicity would boost the reputation of his company and get more people to come to his stores.

As was done in the original experiment, each subject’s responses to the first three questions were averaged together to yield an overall liking rating. (The Cronbach’s alpha for these three liking questions was 0.899, suggesting high statistical coherence.)

the overall liking rating were as follows: Charity = 5.28 (s.e. = 0.19), Advertising = 6.76 (s.e. = 0.12), Charity with Counterfactual = 6.56 (s.e. = 0.17), Advertising with Counterfactual = 5.58 (s.e. = 0.16).

issues.title: Preregistration and analysis code remain unavailable to the reconstruction
issues.reason: The reported preregistration link is no longer usable and the linked analysis code could not be retrieved during source intake.
issues.impact: The exact planned tests and analysis implementation cannot be verified against those files.
issues.suggestedAction: Provide the AsPredicted registration identifier or original R code.

issues.title: Attention check reported without the exact item
issues.reason: The paper reports six attention-check failures. Its text and the available supplement do not supply the item wording or its effect on the final analysis samples.
issues.impact: The original attention check cannot be reconstructed exactly from the available materials.
issues.suggestedAction: Obtain the administered survey item and analysis inclusion rule.

issues.title: Participant and degrees-of-freedom counts do not resolve to an exact analysis sample
issues.reason: The paper reports 501 recruited, six attention-check failures and 149 task-related exclusions in Experiment 2. Simple subtraction gives 346 if both are applied. A conventional equal-variance two-group t(343) would imply 345, while t(495) without exclusions would imply 497. The paper does not give cell counts or enough information to infer which denominator each test used.
issues.impact: The reported effects are preserved, and the Program leaves per-condition analyzed sample sizes blank.
issues.suggestedAction: Verify analyzed counts, exclusion order and test specifications against the original analysis files.

issues.title: The paper plots hiring proportions without exact cells
issues.reason: Figure 4 shows the choice pattern as curves, without printing a table of exact per-level numerators and denominators.
issues.impact: The figure supports the reported pattern. The underlying counts for each point are unavailable.
issues.suggestedAction: Obtain an aggregate table of choice counts by condition and extra amount.

issues.title: Deceptiveness sentence repeats a conflicting mean
issues.reason: The Advertising comparison prints both 3.36 and a repeated 5.06. The plotted points associate 3.36 with Advertising and 5.06 with Charity.
issues.impact: A literal transcription of the repeated number would report the wrong Advertising mean.
issues.suggestedAction: Use Figure 3 when citing the advertising value and retain the text discrepancy.
